transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you. Well, it's kind of a lot, to be honest. I mean, I run my own company, right? Built it from the ground up after I left high school, so I’ve always been used to juggling a million things and just making it work. But what really made me finally come in and make this appointment is that for the past year or so, things have just gotten completely out of hand. 

I just can't seem to stay on track. The absolute smallest things are derailing me now. Like, my phone will buzz—not even ring, just that little vibration on the desk—and I instantly drop what I'm doing. Or somebody will just walk past my office door. We built out the new office space with these glass walls, which seemed like a great idea for, you know, company transparency and culture at the time, but now every single time someone walks by to grab a coffee, my brain just snaps right to them. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around me in the office. It’s my own head, too. I’ll be looking at a critical financial report, really needing to focus, and suddenly I’ll have a completely random thought about my in-laws—like, wondering if my father-in-law is going to bring up that pontoon boat he wants to buy again this weekend—and boom, it just pulls me off what I’m doing before I can even stop it. It’s like my attention is just getting hijacked by literally anything that moves or pops into my head. It's been going on like this for a solid year now, maybe a little more, and it's just exhausting trying to get through a normal workday when every little thing pulls me away.

Alongside this distractibility, do you find yourself frequently worrying excessively about various things—like work, finances, or family—more days than not, even when there's no immediate problem to solve?

No, honestly, that is not really me at all. I mean, sure, running a business means there is always something on the horizon, but I don't just sit around agonizing over hypothetical situations. Like, if there is an actual problem—say, a supply chain issue, which, by the way, has been an absolute nightmare since last quarter because our main distributor in Ohio decided to change their freight company without giving us any heads up, causing a massive three-day delay on literally everything—I just fix it. I get right on the phone, I figure it out, and we move on. I definitely do not lose sleep over things that haven't happened yet or sit around dreading the unknown. 

My wife, now she is a bit of a worrier, always asking what if this happens or what if that happens, especially with the kids' tuition going up again this year, but I always tell her that we will just cross those bridges when we get to them. So, no, I wouldn't say I have that constant worry hanging over me. It is really just the distraction stuff I was talking about. The constant pulling of my attention. But the actual worrying? Nah, I have always been pretty good at just taking things exactly as they come. If I sat around worrying about every single little thing that could possibly go wrong with a company of fifty employees, I never would have made it past that first year when I was just operating out of my buddy's garage back when I was nineteen. So yeah, no excessive worrying here.
Thinking back to when you were a kid in school, did you have similar problems with getting easily distracted or struggling to focus, even before you started your business?

Yeah, actually... looking back, it really was like that when I was a kid, too. I mean, it wasn't just the distraction, though that was definitely there, but it was just... I was always in motion, you know? Always doing something I wasn't supposed to be doing at that exact moment. 

I remember my teachers were constantly—and I mean constantly—moving my seat. Every year, it was the same routine. First week of school, I'd start out somewhere in the middle or the back, and by Friday, I was parked right next to the teacher's desk. And it was because I just talked too much. I couldn't help it. If a thought popped into my head, I had to say it right then and there to whoever was sitting next to me. Didn't matter if the teacher was right in the middle of a lesson on fractions or whatever. 

And getting up... oh man. I'd just stand up and wander over to the pencil sharpener, or go look out the window, or just stretch my legs without ever raising my hand or asking permission. It just didn't even register that I was supposed to wait. It drove Mrs. Gable—she was my fourth-grade teacher, nice lady, wore these huge floral dresses—it drove her absolutely up the wall. 

Plus, I was terrible at waiting for my turn to speak. If the teacher asked a question to the class, I’d just blurt the answer out before they even finished the sentence. I remember once in middle school, my history teacher actually instituted a rule where I wasn't allowed to speak unless I was holding this specific rubber chicken he kept on his desk, just to try and slow me down. So, yeah, it’s not exactly a new thing, this whole struggling to just sit still and focus thing. It’s been there pretty much my whole life, I guess, even before I dropped out and started the business.

As an adult now, do you still notice yourself feeling restless, needing to move around, or blurting things out impulsively—similar to what you described as a kid—or has that physical restlessness mostly settled down?

Yeah, it definitely hasn't gone away. I mean, maybe I'm not wandering around a classroom anymore, but that restless feeling? It's still there, 100 percent. It's almost like... I don't know, like there's this motor running inside of me all the time, just constantly humming in the background, and I can't find the switch to turn it off. 

It gets really obvious when I'm in situations where I'm absolutely supposed to just sit still and be quiet. Like family dinners, for example. My wife's parents come over every Sunday for this big, formal sit-down roast, right? And I love them, I really do, but sitting there at the dining room table for an hour and a half while they talk about their garden or whatever... it is physical torture. I feel this intense need to just get up, or shift around, or at the very least, I have to be doing something with my hands. I'll end up folding my napkin into tiny squares, unfolding it, tearing little pieces off the corner, or spinning my fork around until my wife gives me that look from across the table. 

And it’s the same thing at these church volunteer meetings I got roped into. I’m on the finance committee—which makes sense, given what I do for a living—but these meetings drag on forever. We sit in these uncomfortable folding chairs in the basement, and everyone wants to deliberate for twenty minutes over a fifty-dollar budget item for the youth group bake sale. I literally cannot just sit there. I’m tapping my foot, shifting my weight, clicking my pen over and over until someone glares at me. Sometimes I have to excuse myself to go to the bathroom just so I can walk down the hall and burn off some of that energy, because if I don't, I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my own skin. So yeah, the blurting things out maybe isn't as bad as when I was ten, but that physical need to move? That motor? It's still running just as hot as it ever did.
